source_text: Ut quibus lex data non est, intellegantur non esse praecepta transgressi, rei autem convincantur, quoniam neglegentes rationem, quam proprii in unoquoque protestantur affectus, vel humanae societatis vel pudoris iura temeraverint; atque ideo mutua quidem imitatione, non tamen legis, quae necdum lata erat, dicuntur transgressione peccasse, usque ad legem ergo peccatum fuit, non praevaricatio, post legem autem non solum peccatum, sed etiam praevaricatio. Regnavit autem mors aeterna, quam Adae, si peccasset, ascripturum se Deus spoponderat. Igitur illa mors peccato debita, mors poenalis, regnavit et ante legem in eos, qui peccaverunt, sicut in Sodomitis et in his, qui diluvii tempore propter iniquitatem, voluntariam tamen, vel varia sunt aetate consumpti, regnavit et post legem in his, quos reos praevaricationis invenit.
pass_a_gloss: So that those to whom a law was not given may be understood not to have transgressed precepts, but may be convicted as defendants, since, neglecting reason, which proper affects protest in each one, they have violated the rights either of human society or of shame; and therefore they are said to have sinned by a mutual imitation indeed, not nevertheless by a transgression of the law which had not yet been passed; until the law therefore there was sin, not transgression, but after the law not only sin but also transgression. But eternal death reigned, which God had pledged that he would ascribe to Adam if he had sinned. Therefore that death owed to sin, a penal death, reigned even before the law over those who sinned, as in the Sodomites and in those who at the time of the flood on account of iniquity, yet voluntary, were consumed even at a varied age, it reigned also after the law in those whom it found defendants of transgression.

pass_b_english: Those to whom a law was not given should thus be understood not to have transgressed commands. Yet they are convicted as guilty because, neglecting the reason to which each person’s own feelings bear witness, they violated the rights of human society or of decency. They are therefore said to have sinned by imitating one another, but not by transgressing a law not yet given. Until the law, then, there was sin, not transgression; after the law, not only sin but also transgression. Eternal death reigned, which God had promised to assign to Adam if he sinned (Genesis 2:17). Thus that death owed to sin, that punitive death, reigned before the law over those who sinned: for example, the Sodomites, those destroyed at the time of the flood, and people of various ages destroyed because of wickedness—voluntary wickedness, however (Genesis 6:5–7; Genesis 7:21–23; Genesis 19:24–25). It also reigned after the law over those it found guilty of transgression (Genesis 6:5–7) (Genesis 7:21–23) (Genesis 19:24–25).
